questions.q: Which explanation is best suited to the operators who will phone the flagged customers?
options: The full SHAP beeswarm plot in log-odds
A plain-language list of who to contact and why, using the customer's own values
A proof that the model is causal
questions.explain: Operators need actionable, plain-language reasons per customer, such as a new customer on a monthly contract paying a high price.

questions.q: Why is a default 0.5 cutoff a poor way to decide who gets a retention offer?
options: It has no business meaning; the best cutoff depends on costs and benefits such as offer cost and value of a saved customer
scikit-learn does not allow a cutoff of 0.5
questions.explain: In the lesson, net value kept rising as the cutoff dropped to about 0.2 because each save (60) is worth far more than each offer (10).

questions.q: At a 0.2 cutoff the lesson's table shows 304 customers flagged and 120 caught. What is the precision, roughly?
questions.explain: Precision is caught divided by flagged: 120 / 304 is about 0.39. The strategy still pays because each save is worth much more than each offer costs.

questions.q: Which of these belongs in the Caveats part of a four-part presentation?
options: The assumptions used, what data the model was trained on, and where it may fail
A list of customers to call
questions.explain: Caveats state assumptions, data scope, and known limits, and what would trigger a review. The action part holds owners and dates.

questions.q: Why should you show the cost and save-rate assumptions when presenting the recommended cutoff?
options: Assumptions are irrelevant to the recommendation
Because the best cutoff changes if the assumptions change, and stakeholders should be able to challenge them
questions.explain: The recommendation is only as good as the assumptions behind it, so state them and let decision makers question them.
